title: Ecology
summary: Populations, communities, ecosystems and the biosphere.

layers.basics: Ecology studies how organisms interact with each other and their environment. It scales from one population up to the planet, including energy flow and the cycling of matter.
layers.deeper: Populations grow, compete, are eaten and cooperate; communities have structure and change over time; ecosystems pass energy along food chains and recycle nutrients. Human activity now reshapes all of it.
layers.expert: Ecological theory uses models (logistic growth, Lotka–Volterra) and long-term data. Conservation biology applies this to slow biodiversity loss, balancing evidence, values and policy under uncertainty.

title: Scope of ecology and the niche
summary: Levels of ecological study and what a species needs.

layers.basics: Ecologists study organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems and the biosphere. A species' niche is the set of conditions and resources it uses.
layers.deeper: Abiotic factors (temperature, water, light) and biotic factors (other species) shape where organisms live. Fundamental niche is the potential range, realised niche is what is actually occupied.
layers.expert: Hutchinson's n-dimensional hypervolume formalises niche. Species distribution models predict ranges from climate variables, and can forecast range shifts under warming.

layers.basics: Populations are described by size, density, spacing (clumped, uniform, random) and age structure.
layers.deeper: Mark–recapture and quadrats estimate sizes. Life tables and survivorship curves (Types I, II, III) summarise births and deaths by age.
layers.expert: Net reproductive rate R₀ = Σ lₓmₓ; generation time and intrinsic rate r follow from the Euler–Lotka equation. Type III survivorship (high juvenile mortality) is typical of oysters and many fish.

layers.basics: Without limits, populations grow exponentially. Real populations level off near the carrying capacity K.
layers.deeper: Exponential growth: dN/dt = rN. Logistic: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K). Real populations often overshoot, cycle or crash.
layers.expert: Solution of logistic: N(t) = K/(1 + ((K − N₀)/N₀)e^(−rt)). The discrete-time logistic map (May, 1976) settles to a fixed point for growth parameter r < 3, doubles its period from r = 3, and is chaotic beyond r ≈ 3.57. Time delays in continuous models can also produce oscillations.

title: Life-history strategies and population regulation
summary: Trade-offs between growth, reproduction and survival.

layers.basics: r-selected species make many offspring with little care; K-selected species make few offspring with more care. Density-dependent factors (disease, competition) regulate population size. An African elephant carries one calf for about 22 months, a typical K-selected strategy.
layers.deeper: Weather and disasters act independent of density. Boom–bust cycles such as snowshoe hare–lynx are classic examples; field experiments point to predation and food acting together.
layers.expert: The r/K scheme is a simplification; modern life-history theory uses trade-offs between fecundity and survival. Snowshoe hare cycle period ≈ 10 years.

open_questions: What drives the roughly 10-year snowshoe hare cycle (predation, food shortage, or both) and what drives lemming cycles is still debated.

title: Metapopulations and human population growth
summary: Patches of populations and the human trend.

layers.basics: A metapopulation is a set of local populations linked by migration, where local extinction and recolonisation balance. Human population is ≈ 8.2 billion and growth is slowing.
layers.deeper: The demographic transition describes falling death rates then birth rates. UN medium projections peak near 10.3 billion in the 2080s.
layers.expert: Levins model: dp/dt = cp(1 − p) − ep. Total fertility rate globally ≈ 2.25 (2024); replacement ≈ 2.1. Projections carry substantial uncertainty.

open_questions: How fast fertility will keep falling, and therefore when and at what level world population peaks, is uncertain (UN medium variant about 10.3 billion in the 2080s).

title: Competition and predation models

layers.basics: Species that need the same resources compete. Predators reduce prey numbers, and prey adaptations evolve in response.
layers.deeper: Gause's experiments with Paramecium showed competitive exclusion. Lotka–Volterra equations produce predator–prey cycles.
layers.expert: Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model: dx/dt = αx − βxy, dy/dt = δxy − γy, where x is prey, y is predator, α is the prey growth rate, β the predation rate, δ the conversion of prey into predators and γ the predator death rate. In the separate Lotka–Volterra competition model, dN₁/dt = r₁N₁(1 − (N₁ + α₁₂N₂)/K₁), coexistence requires each species to limit itself more than it limits the other. Resource partitioning allows coexistence (MacArthur's warblers).

formula: dx/dt = αx − βxy;  dy/dt = δxy − γy

layers.basics: Mutualism benefits both partners (bees and flowers), commensalism benefits one without harm, parasitism benefits one at the cost of the other.
layers.deeper: Mycorrhizae, gut microbes, coral–algae and cleaner fish are mutualisms. Parasites include tapeworms, ticks and malaria protists.
layers.expert: Interaction outcomes are context dependent and can shift along a mutualism–parasitism continuum. Parasites alter host behaviour (Toxoplasma in rodents, Ophiocordyceps in ants).

title: Community structure, diversity and keystone species
summary: Who lives together and how many.

layers.basics: A community is all the species in an area. Species richness counts species; evenness describes how equally abundant they are.
layers.deeper: Keystone species (sea otters, wolves, sea stars) affect communities far beyond their abundance. Wolf removal from Yellowstone (1920s) and return (1995) have been linked to changes in elk behaviour and willow and aspen recovery, but how much of this is a true trophic cascade is debated.
layers.expert: Shannon index H = −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ. Paine's Pisaster removal experiment (1966) cut mussel-bed diversity from 15 to 8 species. Species–area relationship S = cA^z with z ≈ 0.15–0.35.

open_questions: How much of the Yellowstone vegetation change is due to wolves, as opposed to climate, hydrology, other predators and hunting, is disputed.

title: Ecological succession and disturbance

layers.basics: After a disturbance such as fire, communities change in a predictable sequence called succession. Primary succession starts on bare rock; secondary succession starts on soil.
layers.deeper: Pioneer species (lichens, grasses) are replaced by shrubs and trees. The intermediate-disturbance hypothesis predicts highest diversity at moderate disturbance; empirical support is mixed.
layers.expert: Climax community concepts are now seen as less deterministic; priority effects and history matter. After the 1980 Mount St. Helens eruption, surviving plants and buried seeds and roots (biological legacies) sped recovery on parts of the blast zone, while the barren pumice plain was colonised slowly by pioneers such as lupines.

facts: predicts a diversity peak; support mixed
open_questions: Whether diversity really peaks at intermediate disturbance, and how often, is debated.

title: Food webs and energy flow
summary: Who eats whom and how energy passes.

layers.basics: Energy enters ecosystems through producers and passes to consumers and decomposers. Most energy is lost as heat at each step.
layers.deeper: Typically about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level (real values vary widely), which is one reason food chains rarely exceed four or five links; ecosystem size and dynamic stability may also play a part. Biomass pyramids narrow upward in most ecosystems.
layers.expert: Trophic transfer efficiency ranges ≈ 5–20%. Net primary production = gross primary production (GPP) minus the producers' own respiration. Aquatic food webs can show inverted biomass pyramids with rapid-turnover producers.

formula: NPP = GPP − Rₐ (Rₐ = respiration of the producers themselves)

title: Primary production and decomposition

layers.basics: Plants and algae make organic matter (primary production). Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil and water.
layers.deeper: Production is highest in tropical rainforests and coral reefs per area; open ocean covers more area but is nutrient-poor.
layers.expert: Limiting nutrients are N and P on land and in freshwater, and iron in high-nutrient low-chlorophyll ocean regions. Decomposition rate depends on temperature, moisture and litter quality (lignin:N).

facts: Ocean share of global NPP (open ocean plus coastal)
≈ 46% (48.5 of 104.9 Pg C/yr; Field et al. 1998)

title: Biogeochemical cycles
summary: Cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water.

layers.basics: Elements cycle between living things and the environment. Carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water each have reservoirs and fluxes.
layers.deeper: Humans have altered these cycles: fossil fuel burning adds CO₂, fertilisers add nitrogen and phosphorus, and runoff causes eutrophication.
layers.expert: Residence times range from days (atmospheric water ≈ 9 d) to millions of years (rock P). Human creation of reactive nitrogen (≈ 210 Tg N/yr, about 120 of it by the Haber–Bosch process) is several times natural terrestrial biological fixation (≈ 58 Tg N/yr, range 40–100).

title: Terrestrial and aquatic biomes

layers.basics: Biomes are large regions with typical climate and life: tundra, taiga, temperate forest, grassland, desert, tropical forest, plus freshwater and marine systems.
layers.deeper: Temperature and precipitation largely predict a land biome (Whittaker diagram). Oceans are divided by depth and light into zones.
layers.expert: Marine habitats include intertidal, pelagic, benthic, abyssal and hydrothermal vent communities (chemosynthesis). Biome shifts under climate change are already observed at treelines and coral reefs.

facts: large share, often quoted as about half; poorly quantified because many tropical groups are undescribed

title: Biogeography and island biogeography

layers.basics: The distribution of species reflects climate, geography and history. Islands hold fewer species than mainlands, and larger or closer islands hold more.
layers.deeper: MacArthur and Wilson's equilibrium theory (1967) balances immigration and extinction rates.
layers.expert: Latitudinal diversity gradient (more species near the equator) has multiple proposed causes (energy, area, time, speciation rates). Wallace Line and plate tectonics explain faunal differences.

open_questions: Why species richness peaks in the tropics (energy, area, time, speciation and extinction rates) is unresolved.

title: Climate change and ecological impacts
summary: How warming and CO₂ affect life.

layers.basics: Rising temperature and CO₂ are shifting ranges, seasons and ecosystems. Oceans are warming and becoming more acidic.
layers.deeper: Coral bleaching, phenological mismatches and species range shifts are documented. Ocean pH has fallen by ≈ 0.1 since pre-industrial times.
layers.expert: Long-term global warming is ≈ 1.3 °C above the 1850–1900 average (WMO assessment for 2024), and the single year 2024 was ≈ 1.55 °C above it. Impacts depend on adaptation capacity, dispersal, and interactions; tipping points (Amazon dieback, coral loss) are assessed with uncertainty.

open_questions: Where ecological tipping points (Amazon dieback, coral reef loss) lie, and how fast species can adapt or disperse, remain uncertain.

title: Biodiversity and the extinction crisis
summary: Why diversity matters and how it is lost.

layers.basics: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. It is declining mainly through habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change.
layers.deeper: IUCN assesses extinction risk (Least Concern to Extinct). About 28% of assessed species are threatened. Monitored vertebrate populations declined by an average of ≈ 73% from 1970 to 2020 (Living Planet Index, 2024). This tracks the average change across monitored populations, not the loss of total animal numbers.
layers.expert: Estimated extinction rates are ≈ 10–1,000× background depending on method. The Living Planet Index is debated methodologically. Global ecosystem-service value estimates (pollination, water purification and more) are of order $100 trillion per year (Costanza et al. 2014: $125 trillion for 2011), but they depend heavily on assumptions.

open_questions: How fast species are going extinct today depends strongly on method (10–1000× background), and the Living Planet Index methodology is debated.

layers.basics: Conservation tools include protected areas, habitat restoration, species recovery plans, anti-poaching efforts and managing invasive species.
layers.deeper: Corridors link habitats. Reintroductions such as gray wolves to Yellowstone and California condor breeding programs show recovery is possible.
layers.expert: Population viability analysis estimates extinction risk; 30×30 targets aim to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030. Invasive alien species cost the global economy more than US$423 billion a year (2019, IPBES 2023), a figure widely regarded as an underestimate.

title: Ecosystem services and ecological economics

layers.basics: Ecosystems provide food, clean water, pollination, climate regulation and recreation, which have large economic and cultural value.
layers.deeper: Wetlands filter water and buffer floods; pollinators matter most for fruit, nut and vegetable crops.
layers.expert: Valuation uses market prices, avoided costs and stated preference methods and is controversial; Costanza et al. estimated $125–145 trillion per year in 2007 US dollars (2014, depending on the scenario), a disputed order-of-magnitude figure.

facts: $125 trillion/yr for 2011 (unit values and biome areas updated) or $145 trillion/yr (unit values only); disputed
Crops that depend at least partly on animal pollinators
≈ 35% of global crop production by volume; total loss of pollinators would cut production ≈ 3–8%
open_questions: Monetary valuation of ecosystem services is methodologically contested and highly assumption-dependent.

title: Biostatistics and quantitative biology
summary: Statistics, modelling and data analysis for biologists.

layers.basics: Biological data are noisy, so conclusions need statistics. Describing data, estimating uncertainty and testing ideas fairly are core lab skills.
layers.deeper: Probability distributions model variation; confidence intervals and hypothesis tests quantify evidence; regression and ANOVA relate variables; differential equations model change in populations and cells.
layers.expert: Good practice includes design before analysis, awareness of multiple testing, effect sizes, reproducible code and honest reporting. Mechanistic models (ODEs, stochastic simulation) complement statistical ones.

layers.basics: Mean, median, standard deviation and range summarise a data set; histograms and box plots show its shape.
layers.deeper: The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is not. Standard error (SD/√n) describes the precision of a mean.
layers.expert: Sample variance uses n − 1 for an unbiased estimate. Report SD for spread of data and SE or CI for uncertainty of the mean; error bars must be labelled.

title: Common distributions: binomial, Poisson, normal
summary: Models for biological counts and measurements.

layers.basics: The binomial counts successes in n trials (offspring with a trait), the Poisson counts rare events (mutations per genome), and the normal describes many continuous traits.
layers.deeper: The Poisson variance equals its mean; for large n the binomial is approximately normal. About 95% of a normal population lies within ±1.96 SD.
layers.expert: Luria–Delbrück (1943) found far more variance in resistant-colony counts between cultures than a Poisson distribution predicts, with occasional 'jackpot' cultures, showing that mutations arise spontaneously before selection rather than being induced by it. Overdispersed counts are better modelled by negative binomial.

title: Sampling and the central limit theorem
summary: Why sample means are nearly normal.

layers.basics: Means of large random samples are approximately normally distributed, whatever the original distribution, centred on the true mean.
layers.deeper: The spread of sample means (standard error) shrinks as 1/√n, so larger samples give more precise estimates.
layers.expert: CLT requires finite variance and independent samples; heavy-tailed data or strong dependence (spatial or temporal autocorrelation) violate it. Bootstrapping provides an alternative.

facts: ≈ 30 (depends on skew: strongly skewed data need far more)

title: Confidence intervals
summary: Range of plausible values for a parameter.

layers.basics: A 95% confidence interval is computed so that 95% of such intervals from repeated experiments would contain the true value.
layers.deeper: It is typically mean ± t × SE. A wider interval means more uncertainty.
layers.expert: It is not "95% probability the parameter is in this interval" for a given interval (frequentist). Bayesian credible intervals give that interpretation under a prior.

layers.basics: A hypothesis test asks how surprising the data would be if there were no effect (the null hypothesis). The p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of getting results at least as extreme as those observed.
layers.deeper: A small p (< 0.05 by convention) suggests the data are unlikely under the null. Type I error is a false positive; Type II is a false negative.
layers.expert: p-values are not the probability the null is true, and are not effect sizes. Power = 1 − β. Misuse (p-hacking, publication bias) contributes to the replication crisis.

layers.basics: A t-test compares a sample mean with a value, or two group means, accounting for the variability and sample size.
layers.deeper: Types: one-sample, two-sample (independent), paired (same subjects before and after). Welch's test does not assume equal variances.
layers.expert: Student (W. S. Gosset) derived the t distribution in 1908 while working at Guinness. Assumes approximate normality; for small, skewed samples, rank-based tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired data, Mann–Whitney for two independent groups) test a shift in distribution rather than a difference in means.

layers.basics: A chi-square test compares observed counts with those expected, such as the 9:3:3:1 ratio in a dihybrid cross.
layers.deeper: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. A large value means a poor fit. It is also used to test whether two categorical variables are related.
layers.expert: Degrees of freedom: categories − 1 (goodness of fit) or (r − 1)(c − 1). Expected counts should be ≥ 5. For 3 df, the 5% critical value is 7.81.

layers.basics: ANOVA tests whether any of three or more group means differ, by comparing variation between groups with variation within groups.
layers.deeper: A significant F is followed by post-hoc tests (Tukey) to find which groups differ. Running many t-tests inflates false positives.
layers.expert: F = MS_between/MS_within. Assumes independence, normal residuals and equal variances. Mixed-effects models handle repeated measures and nested designs (e.g., cells within animals).

layers.basics: Correlation measures how closely two variables move together (−1 to +1). Linear regression fits a line to predict one variable from another.
layers.deeper: Correlation does not prove causation. R² is the fraction of variance explained, and residual plots check the fit.
layers.expert: Ordinary least squares minimises squared residuals. Extensions: multiple, logistic (binary outcomes), Poisson and mixed models. Extrapolation beyond data and confounding are common errors.

layers.basics: If you test 20 hypotheses at p < 0.05, you expect about one false positive by chance alone.
layers.deeper: Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests; the false discovery rate (Benjamini–Hochberg) controls the share of false positives among hits.
layers.expert: Genomic studies test 10⁴–10⁶ hypotheses; thresholds such as 5×10⁻⁸ (GWAS) or FDR < 5% (RNA-seq) are used. Pre-registration reduces analytic flexibility.

title: Experimental design and power
summary: Planning to get a clear answer.

layers.basics: Good design uses randomisation, replication, controls and blocking. Sample size should be chosen before the experiment.
layers.deeper: Pseudoreplication occurs when non-independent samples are treated as independent. Power analysis estimates the needed n for a chosen effect size.
layers.expert: Sample size n ≈ 2(z₁₋α/₂ + z₁₋β)²σ²/δ² per group. Randomised block, factorial and split-plot designs increase efficiency; ethical design aims to minimise animals and participants (3Rs).

layers.basics: Bayes' theorem combines prior knowledge with data to give an updated (posterior) probability. It is used in diagnostics, genetics and phylogenetics.
layers.deeper: A positive test for a rare disease may still be most likely a false positive. Example: sensitivity 99%, specificity 95%, prevalence 1% gives ≈ 17% chance of disease after a positive test.
layers.expert: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. MCMC samples posteriors for complex models; prior choice matters for small data. Used in BEAST (phylogenetics), STRUCTURE (populations) and clinical trial adaptive designs.

layers.basics: Rates of change in biology are modelled with differential equations: growth dN/dt, enzyme reactions, drug decay and epidemics.
layers.deeper: First-order decay dC/dt = −kC gives half-life t½ = ln2/k. Michaelis–Menten and logistic models are nonlinear ODEs.
layers.expert: Equilibria and stability come from linearisation (eigenvalues of the Jacobian). Systems such as the SIR model, Lotka–Volterra and gene-circuit toggles show oscillations, bistability and bifurcations; numeric solvers (RK4) handle cases without closed form.

title: Matrix population models

layers.basics: A matrix tracks how many individuals are in each age or stage class and projects them forward one step at a time.
layers.deeper: The dominant eigenvalue λ gives the long-term growth rate: λ > 1 growth, λ < 1 decline.
layers.expert: Elasticity analysis shows which vital rates most affect λ; for loggerhead sea turtles, λ is most sensitive to survival of large juveniles (then small juveniles and adults), not to egg or hatchling survival, which pointed to turtle excluder devices in shrimp trawls (Crouse et al. 1987; Crowder et al. 1994). Stochastic and density-dependent extensions exist.

facts: large-juvenile survival (then small juveniles and adults)

title: Data analysis, programming and reproducibility

layers.basics: Biologists increasingly write code in R or Python to analyse and plot data, and keep scripts and data organised so others can repeat the work.
layers.deeper: Version control (git), notebooks and workflow managers (Snakemake, Nextflow) support reproducibility. FAIR data principles: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable.
layers.expert: Common failure modes: undocumented data cleaning, hidden manual steps, non-seeded random numbers and software-version drift. Containers (Docker) fix environments; code review catches errors.

facts: ≈ 70% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment; more than half failed to reproduce their own

title: Lab skills and research practice
summary: Hands-on techniques, safety, data handling and research ethics.

layers.basics: Biology is learned at the bench as well as in books. This section covers microscopes, solutions, instruments, culture, safety and honest record-keeping.
layers.deeper: Good technique makes data trustworthy: accurate pipetting, clean sterile work, calibrated instruments, careful notes. Safety rules and ethics keep people, animals and the public protected.
layers.expert: Experiments need controls, calibration and documentation to be repeatable. Regulatory frameworks (IBC, IRB, IACUC, biosafety levels) formalise responsible practice.

layers.basics: Wear gloves, eye protection and a lab coat; know where eyewash, showers and exits are; never eat or drink in the lab; dispose of waste correctly.
layers.deeper: Biosafety levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4) match containment to the hazard. Most teaching labs are BSL-1 or BSL-2.
layers.expert: BSL-3 requires controlled access and directional airflow for agents like M. tuberculosis; BSL-4 (Ebola, Marburg) uses full-body suits or Class III cabinets. Risk assessment weighs agent, procedure and host factors.

layers.basics: A compound microscope uses lenses to magnify cells. Total magnification is eyepiece × objective, and resolution limits detail.
layers.deeper: Phase-contrast and DIC reveal unstained living cells; bright-field needs staining (Gram, H&E) for good contrast.
layers.expert: Abbe limit: d = λ/(2NA) ≈ 200 nm for visible light and NA ≈ 1.4. Oil immersion raises NA. Resolution, not magnification, decides what can be seen.

layers.basics: Fluorescent dyes or proteins (like GFP) glow when lit with the right colour, showing where specific molecules are in cells.
layers.deeper: Confocal microscopes block out-of-focus light for sharp sections. Live-cell imaging tracks proteins over time.
layers.expert: Super-resolution methods (STED, PALM/STORM; Nobel 2014) reach ≈ 20–50 nm. Photobleaching and phototoxicity limit imaging; careful controls avoid artefacts from overexpression.

title: Electron microscopy and cryo-EM

layers.basics: Electron microscopes use electron beams to see detail far smaller than light microscopes: TEM shows interior slices, SEM shows surfaces.
layers.deeper: The beam path must be in vacuum, so conventional samples are chemically fixed, dehydrated and stained; cryo-EM instead flash-freezes samples in vitreous ice, but they are still imaged in vacuum. Images are grey-scale.
layers.expert: Instrument resolution of aberration-corrected electron microscopes is below 0.1 nm (atomic columns 45 pm apart have been resolved in crystalline physical samples), while biological specimens are limited to much coarser detail by preparation and radiation damage; cryo-EM reconstructs structures to near-atomic resolution from thousands of frozen particle images (Nobel 2017).

facts: below 0.1 nm (aberration-corrected, crystalline physical specimens); biological specimens much coarser

title: Pipetting and preparing solutions

layers.basics: Micropipettes deliver exact microlitre volumes. Pipette with the right range, pre-wet tips and dispense steadily.
layers.deeper: To make a solution: calculate mass from molarity × volume × molar mass, dissolve, adjust pH and bring to final volume.
layers.expert: Error sources: temperature, viscosity, angle and speed. Calibration checks gravimetrically. Serial dilutions propagate error; a 1:10 series of 6 steps spans 10⁶.

facts: depends on volume; worst at the bottom of the range (see the manufacturer datasheet)

layers.basics: A spectrophotometer measures how much light a solution absorbs. Absorbance is proportional to concentration.
layers.deeper: DNA is quantified at 260 nm (A260 of 1.0 ≈ 50 µg/mL dsDNA); proteins at 280 nm or by colour assays (Bradford, BCA).
layers.expert: A = ε·l·c, valid up to A ≈ 1–2. NADH absorbs at 340 nm (ε = 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹), used to follow dehydrogenase kinetics. Blanks and standard curves correct for background.

layers.basics: A centrifuge spins samples so heavier components sink. Differential centrifugation separates nuclei, mitochondria and membranes.
layers.deeper: Speed is given as relative centrifugal force (× g), not rpm. Density gradients separate similar particles.
layers.expert: RCF = 1.118×10⁻⁵ · r · rpm². Meselson–Stahl used CsCl density-gradient centrifugation to show semiconservative replication. Ultracentrifuges reach ≈ 10⁶ × g.

layers.basics: Cells are grown in flasks or dishes with nutrient medium at 37 °C and 5% CO₂. Aseptic technique, working in a biosafety cabinet and sterilising tools, prevents contamination.
layers.deeper: Primary cells have limited life; immortal lines (HeLa, from 1951) grow indefinitely. Cultures are checked for mycoplasma.
layers.expert: Cell line misidentification is well documented (the ICLAC register lists hundreds of misidentified lines), so authentication (STR profiling) is needed. HeLa raised ethical issues about consent; Henrietta Lacks' family was acknowledged in later agreements.

layers.basics: Green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish can be attached to other proteins to see where and when they appear in a living cell.
layers.deeper: Reporters such as GFP, luciferase and lacZ show gene activity. Variants cover the whole colour range.
layers.expert: GFP forms its chromophore autocatalytically from Ser65–Tyr66–Gly67 with oxygen; Nobel 2008 (Shimomura, Chalfie, Tsien). Tags can change protein behaviour, so controls are needed.

title: Lab notebooks, data and reports

layers.basics: Record what you did and saw, with dates, in a notebook so others can repeat it. Reports follow IMRaD: introduction, methods, results and discussion.
layers.deeper: Figures need labelled axes with units, error bars and legends. Raw data should be saved unaltered.
layers.expert: Good practice: pre-specify analyses, record software versions and instrument settings, store data in open formats and deposit in repositories. Image manipulation beyond uniform adjustments is misconduct.

facts: set by funder and institution; commonly several years after a project ends

title: Reading and citing scientific literature

layers.basics: Primary papers report original experiments; reviews summarise a field. PubMed and Google Scholar help find them.
layers.deeper: Read the abstract and figures first, then the methods and discussion critically. Peer review is a check but does not guarantee correctness.
layers.expert: Evaluate effect sizes, sample sizes, controls and conflicts of interest; be aware of preprints, retractions and predatory journals. Cite sources properly to avoid plagiarism.

facts: > 10,000 (Nature analysis; inflated by mass retractions at one publisher)

title: Research ethics: IRB, IACUC and misconduct
summary: Rules that protect participants, animals and honesty.

layers.basics: Research with people needs informed consent and review by an Institutional Review Board (IRB); animal research needs approval by an IACUC.
layers.deeper: Misconduct means fabrication, falsification and plagiarism. The Tuskegee study and Nuremberg trials led to modern human-subject protections (Belmont Report 1979).
layers.expert: The 3Rs (replace, reduce, refine) guide animal work. Dual-use research and gain-of-function work add biosecurity review. Genomic data raise privacy and consent issues, as does editing of human embryos.

title: Field sampling methods

layers.basics: Field biologists use quadrats, transects, traps and cameras. They record location, weather and time and avoid disturbing habitats.
layers.deeper: Random or stratified sampling avoids bias; mark–recapture estimates populations.
layers.expert: Detection probability must be modelled (occupancy models). Permits and ethics approvals are needed; environmental DNA and acoustic monitoring reduce disturbance.

facts: depends on how detectable the target species is
